Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Double Sound Update Rate
Metadata.Note: The sound engine (FromSoftware's MagicOrchestra over FMOD) takes the game's sound orders, a sound started, stopped or moved, once every MainThreadUpdateTime microseconds of its setup text: 33333, 30 times a second, whatever the frame rate. This halves the number that is there, so the orders are taken twice as often: 60 times a second, and 120 where another patch (Bloodborne's 60 FPS++) has made it 60 already. A sound the game starts waits half as long to be taken up. Found by the text itself, so every version of the game that has the line gets it.

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Lower Audio Latency
Metadata.Note: FMOD mixes the game's sound ahead of the speakers in blocks of 256 samples and keeps 4 of them: 1024 samples, 21 milliseconds, between a sound being mixed and being heard. This makes it keep 2, the fewest FMOD takes: 512 samples, 11 milliseconds. Blocks cannot be shorter than 256 samples, the console's smallest. If the sound crackles, the mixer is not keeping up with 2: turn this off. Found by FMOD's own code, so every version of the game that has it gets it.

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Job Wait Pause
Metadata.Note: The game's job system waits for its worker threads in four loops that read a flag or a counter over and over as fast as the CPU can, with nothing in between: in a profile, the main thread spent much of its time in one of them. This puts a PAUSE instruction (the CPU's own hint that a loop is waiting on another thread) in each, where the loop starts again: the loop waits as long as it did, but leaves more of the core to the other thread on it (with Hyper-Threading or SMT) and draws less power, and the CPU does not have to undo what it guessed ahead when the wait ends. Nothing else is changed: each PAUSE takes the place of padding the compiler left there, and each loop's jump back goes to it. Found by the game's own code, so every version of the game that has these loops gets it.

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Highest Model Detail Everywhere
Metadata.GroupNote: How much detail models are drawn with. The game picks one of three detail levels for each model from its distance; each choice shifts that pick, the same way, everywhere. Found by the game's own code, so every version of the game that has it gets it.
Metadata.Note: Every model is drawn with its most detailed mesh, and its full-detail textures, at any distance: the offset is -2. It costs GPU time: more triangles far away. The game has three detail levels per model, 0 (full) to 2, picked from the distances of the model's LodBank param row, then shifted by one offset of the game's own and kept within 0 to 2. It does that in five places, for the different kinds of model; this sets the offset in all five, parts with no LodBank row among them. Found by the game's own code, so every version of the game that has it gets it (the place shadPS4's Model LOD patches by Kyo and auser1337 changed is one of the five).

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Lower Model Detail Everywhere
Metadata.Note: Every model drops one detail level sooner: the offset is 1, so a model drawn at full detail is drawn at level 1, and one at level 1 at level 2. Faster, less detail. The game has three detail levels per model, 0 (full) to 2, picked from the distances of the model's LodBank param row, then shifted by one offset of the game's own and kept within 0 to 2. It does that in five places, for the different kinds of model; this sets the offset in all five, parts with no LodBank row among them. Found by the game's own code, so every version of the game that has it gets it (the place shadPS4's Model LOD patches by Kyo and auser1337 changed is one of the five).

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Lowest Model Detail Everywhere
Metadata.Note: Every model is drawn with its least detailed mesh at any distance: the offset is 2. The fastest, the least detail. The game has three detail levels per model, 0 (full) to 2, picked from the distances of the model's LodBank param row, then shifted by one offset of the game's own and kept within 0 to 2. It does that in five places, for the different kinds of model; this sets the offset in all five, parts with no LodBank row among them. Found by the game's own code, so every version of the game that has it gets it (the place shadPS4's Model LOD patches by Kyo and auser1337 changed is one of the five).

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Frame Rate 30, Lower Input Delay
Metadata.GroupNote: The game's frame rate, in place of its 30. Each choice shows frames as soon as they are done and turns the game's frame skipping off; above 30 the game's timing (physics, animation, camera, effects, the sound engine) is fixed for the rate, and the core runs the frontend and the console's vblanks at it, so nothing else needs setting. Match display takes the display's refresh rate. A change applies at the next start of the game.
Metadata.Note: The game's own 30 frames a second, shown as soon as each is done instead of waiting for every other vblank, and without its frame skipping: the input reaches the screen sooner. shadPS4's 30 FPS++.
Metadata.Author: Kyo

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Frame Rate
Metadata.Note: The game at a steady frame rate above its 30: frames shown as soon as each is done, its frame skipping off, and the game's timing (physics, animation, camera, effects, the sound engine's update) fixed for the rate. Match display takes the display's own refresh rate. The core runs the frontend and the console's vblanks at the rate, so there is nothing else to set. shadPS4's 60 to 960 FPS++, made one patch: the values that change with the rate are worked out from it, which gives rates they did not have, such as 144 and 165, exactly as theirs at the rates they had. Beyond theirs: the game's parts that are stepped each frame by a time handed to them (fifty of them: FPS++ gave 49 1/60 at every rate and one the rate's frame) step by the frame's own time, the one the world steps by, so they keep pace with it at any rate and when frames come late; the cloth's stiffness (it is solved once more each frame, so it was pulled harder the higher the rate; now as hard per second as at 30), the shortest fade of effects and two other one-frame times (a frame at the rate, not 1/60 or 1/30), a per-frame budget (one frame's share), and how fast the stick turns the model in the character creator.
Metadata.Author: Kyo

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Uncapped Frame Rate
Metadata.Note: No frame rate cap: the game runs as fast as it is drawn, up to the display's refresh rate, which the core runs the frontend and the console's vblanks at. The game steps by the time each frame really took (at most 1/30 of a second, so below 30 frames a second it slows down rather than jumps), as in the Frame Rate patches. The timers Uncap FPS++ sets for 120 or 60 frames a second are set for the display's rate instead, as the Frame Rate patches set them; what the Frame Rate patches add beyond FPS++ is here too: the fifty parts stepped each frame step by each frame's real time, the rest follows the display's rate; the follow camera is the Frame Rate patches' (the game's own chase rates, turned into each frame's share by the frame's real time; Uncap FPS++ had halved the rates for 60 and capped the frame time at 1/60, so below 60 frames a second the camera lagged); eleven countdowns Uncap FPS++ made 60 are the game's 30 again (they count seconds down by each frame's time, so they were twice as long); a few values are still those of 60 frames a second, so not recommended. shadPS4's Uncap FPS++.
Metadata.Author: Lance McDonald (manfightdragon), Kyo

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Shadow Map Resolution Highest
Metadata.GroupNote: Shadow detail. The game's graphics settings are kept per area, in its graphics param files (param/drawparam, one for each map and each of its lighting variants), and each area picks its own. These choices change the values in those files as the game reads them: the game's own settings, with no code changed, in every version of the game. Each choice raises a setting to a level the game itself uses in some of its areas, so nothing is asked of the engine that it does not do somewhere already. A change applies at the next start of the game.
Metadata.Note: Every area's shadows drawn into the largest shadow map the game uses: Shadow Map Resolution 3, which most areas have; the areas set to 0 get 3 too. More GPU time and memory where it was 0, nothing elsewhere. What the steps between 0 and 3 are in pixels is not known.

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Shadow Distance x1.5
Metadata.GroupNote: How far shadows are drawn. The game's graphics settings are kept per area, in its graphics param files (param/drawparam, one for each map and each of its lighting variants), and each area picks its own. These choices change the values in those files as the game reads them: the game's own settings, with no code changed, in every version of the game. Each choice raises a setting to a level the game itself uses in some of its areas, so nothing is asked of the engine that it does not do somewhere already. A change applies at the next start of the game.
Metadata.Note: Shadows reach 1.5 times as far before they fade: the far cascades (Cascade Dist 1->2 and 2->3) and the fade (Far Fade Start, Far Fade Dist) of every area are multiplied by 1.5. The nearest cascade is left as it is, so shadows near the player keep their detail; the far ones are spread over more ground, so they are coarser. Best with Shadow Quality at Highest.

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Depth of Field Quality High
Metadata.GroupNote: The quality of the depth of field blur, from Silicon Studio's Yebis, the game's post-processing. The game's graphics settings are kept per area, in its graphics param files (param/drawparam, one for each map and each of its lighting variants), and each area picks its own. These choices change the values in those files as the game reads them: the game's own settings, with no code changed, in every version of the game. Each choice raises a setting to a level the game itself uses in some of its areas, so nothing is asked of the engine that it does not do somewhere already. A change applies at the next start of the game.
Metadata.Note: Depth of field (the blur of what is out of focus) at Yebis' DepthOfFieldQuality 8 at least, in every area: areas set lower are raised to 8, the game's areas use 1 to 12. That a higher number is a finer blur is read from its name; it is not confirmed.

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Depth of Field Quality Highest
Metadata.Note: Depth of field (the blur of what is out of focus) at Yebis' DepthOfFieldQuality 12, the highest any of the game's areas has, in every area. That a higher number is a finer blur is read from its name; it is not confirmed.

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Bloom Quality High
Metadata.GroupNote: The quality of the glow around bright lights (bloom and glare), from Yebis. The game's graphics settings are kept per area, in its graphics param files (param/drawparam, one for each map and each of its lighting variants), and each area picks its own. These choices change the values in those files as the game reads them: the game's own settings, with no code changed, in every version of the game. A change applies at the next start of the game.
Metadata.Note: Bloom and glare (the glow around lights) at Yebis' GlareQuality 5 at least and 8 glare levels at least, in every area: the game's areas use 1 to 7 and 3 to 16. That higher numbers are finer is read from their names; it is not confirmed.

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Bloom Quality Highest
Metadata.Note: Bloom and glare (the glow around lights) at Yebis' GlareQuality 7, the highest any area has, and 8 glare levels at least, in every area. The 16 levels a few areas have are left to those. That higher numbers are finer is read from their names; it is not confirmed.

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Motion Blur Quality High
Metadata.GroupNote: How finely motion blur is sampled, from Yebis. It does not turn motion blur on or off or change its strength. The game's graphics settings are kept per area, in its graphics param files (param/drawparam, one for each map and each of its lighting variants), and each area picks its own. These choices change the values in those files as the game reads them: the game's own settings, with no code changed, in every version of the game. Each choice raises a setting to a level the game itself uses in some of its areas, so nothing is asked of the engine that it does not do somewhere already. A change applies at the next start of the game.
Metadata.Note: Motion blur with 5 samples at least and 4 passes at least (NumBaseSamples, MaxRecurrences), in every area: smoother, less banded blur. The game's areas use 3 to 7 samples and 0 to 5 passes. Where and how much the game blurs is not changed: motion blur stays on where it is on, off where it is off, and as long as it was.

Metadata.Title: Bloodborne
Metadata.Name: Motion Blur Quality Highest
Metadata.Note: Motion blur with 7 samples and 5 passes (NumBaseSamples, MaxRecurrences), the most any area has, in every area: the smoothest blur, the most GPU time. Where and how much the game blurs is not changed: motion blur stays on where it is on, off where it is off, and as long as it was.

Metadata.Note: The ambient occlusion (the shading in corners and creases) of the areas that have EnableUpScale on (14 of the game's 93 SSAO settings), turned off, so it would be worked out at full resolution rather than scaled up. Read from the field's name only; what it does is not confirmed.
